DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026

The arithmetic in the document is correct. The £810 a week, the £42,120 a year and the competitor midpoints all check out. However, the two central claims in your description don't hold up against the document's own data:
- The mushroom risotto has the **strongest** margin on the menu, not the weakest.
- The £42,000 gain ignores the 12% beef cost rise that the paper itself reports.

Correcting both changes the size of the financial case and reverses the risotto decision.

## Major issues

### 1. The risotto has the best margin, not the worst

From Table 1:

| Dish | Margin | Gross profit per plate |
|---|---|---|
| Mushroom risotto | **80%** (highest) | £11.20 |
| Chicken curry | 75% | £10.90 |
| Beef burger | 72% | £10.80 |
| Fish and chips | 69% | £11.40 |
| Sirloin steak | 60% (lowest) | £15.60 |

- By margin percentage, the risotto is the best main on the menu. By cash profit per plate, it beats both the curry and the burger.
- "Lowest sales" is only a tie: the risotto and the specials both sell 90 plates a week.
- The proposed replacement is a seasonal special, and the specials currently run at **64%** margin. A £14 special at that margin earns about £8.96 a plate against the risotto's £11.20. That loses roughly **£200 a week (about £10,500 a year)** if volumes are unchanged.
- The risotto is also, as far as the table shows, the only standing vegetarian main. That matters for group bookings.

The data support keeping the risotto, or at least defining a replacement that matches its margin before removing it.

### 2. The beef price rise isn't in the projection

Section 4 says beef rises 12% on 1 April, the same day the new prices start. Section 5.3 then calculates the gain as if food costs stay flat.

As an upper bound, assuming the whole plate cost were beef:

| | Extra cost per plate | Weekly |
|---|---|---|
| Burger | £4.20 × 12% ≈ £0.50 | ~£131 |
| Steak | £10.40 × 12% ≈ £1.25 | ~£150 |
| **Total** | | **up to ~£280 a week (~£14,600 a year)** |

The real figure is lower, because buns, chips and sides aren't beef, but it's material either way. Much of the burger and steak increase is simply recovering the cost rise, not new profit.

### 3. The net effect is much smaller than £42,000

Combining the two points above, with volumes held constant:

| | Weekly |
|---|---|
| Price increases | +£810 |
| Beef cost rise (upper bound) | −£280 |
| Risotto replaced by a 64%-margin special | −£200 |
| **Net** | **about +£330 (≈ £17,000 a year)** |

The true figure probably sits somewhere between £17,000 and £30,000 a year, depending on the beef share of each plate and what the special earns. That is still positive and still worth doing, but it's not £42,000.

### 4. The 71% margin figure ignores the cost rise, and the margin problem may lie elsewhere

My reconstruction of the main-course margin, excluding the specials (whose prices aren't given):
- **Today:** about 69.9%.
- **After the price rises:** about 71.3%. This matches the paper, but only if costs stay flat.
- **After the beef rise (upper bound):** about 69.7%, roughly where it is now.

There's also a more basic point. Mains are already running at about 70%, yet overall food margin has slipped to 67%. That suggests the erosion is mainly in starters, desserts or sides. The paper would be stronger if it identified where the three points went before fixing mains.

## Smaller issues

- **Trading days.** Section 8 says "six trading days a week," but section 2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is five. The weekly figures are unaffected, but it's an error in the recommendation the owners will read.
- **Monitoring baseline.**
  - Comparing April–May against January–February will confuse the price effect with seasonal change. Spring trade, and Easter in early April, will differ from winter regardless of price.
  - Better comparisons would be the same weeks in 2025, or the unchanged dishes (curry, specials) used as a control.
  - The plan also sets no threshold or action. You should decide in advance what drop in volume would trigger a rethink.
- **Volume headroom isn't quantified.** Ignoring the beef rise, volumes could fall about 8% on fish and burgers and about 11% on steak before gross profit drops. After the beef rise, the burger and steak headroom shrinks to roughly 4–5%. This is the real measure of risk, and it belongs in the paper.
- **The loyalty argument cuts both ways.** A 60% repeat base means most guests *know* the old prices and are the ones most likely to notice. Loyalty isn't the same as price insensitivity.
- **Evidence from 2024.** "No visible effect on bookings" is weak evidence. Bookings could hold while guests trade down from steak to curry, which would only show in dish-level data.
- **Competitor check.** It covers three dishes at five restaurants, which is reasonable but not a "full" check. The curry and risotto weren't compared.
- **Lunch trade.** Weekday lunch is described as "a small share," but no figure is given. Friday and Saturday dinner make up just under half of covers, so the other eight sessions make up the rest. Lunch may be bigger than implied.

## What holds up

- The table figures are internally consistent: the margins match the prices and costs, and the plate counts sum to 1,050.
- All three new prices do sit below the competitor midpoints (£17.98, £16.50 and £29.50), and the current prices are the lowest in the group.
- The case for raising the burger and steak prices is actually *stronger* than the paper makes it, because without an increase the beef rise would cut their margins.

## Suggested revisions

1. Drop the risotto removal, or reframe it as a trial special that must match about 80% margin.
2. Restate the projection net of the beef increase, as a range, with a break-even volume for each dish.
3. Correct "six trading days" to five.
4. Change the monitoring baseline to the same period last year, set a trigger threshold, and track substitution between dishes.
5. Add a line on where the overall margin erosion is coming from, beyond mains.

With those changes, the price increases are still a sensible recommendation. "Low-risk and well evidenced" would only be fair after the corrections.
